target: Daeth e â blodau i'w wraig.
english: He brought flowers for his wife.
tip: ‘dod â’ (literally come with) means bring: ‘daeth e â blodau’ = he brought flowers.

target: Roedd hi wedi gadael cyn i fi gyrraedd.
english: She had left before I arrived.
tip: before I arrived uses ‘cyn i fi’ plus a softened verb: ‘cyrraedd’ becomes ‘gyrraedd’, giving ‘cyn i fi gyrraedd’.

target: Mae'r hydref yma wedi bod yn sychach na'r llynedd.
english: This autumn has been drier than last year.
tip: Add ‘-ach’ for more and ‘na’ for than: ‘sych’ (dry) becomes ‘sychach’, and ‘sychach na'r llynedd’ = drier than last year.

target: Dylwn i fwyta'n iach.
english: I should eat healthily.
tip: ‘dylwn i’ means I should and softens the verb: ‘bwyta’ becomes ‘fwyta’, so ‘dylwn i fwyta’ = I should eat.

target: Roedd llais hyfryd ganddi.
english: She had a beautiful voice.
tip: Welsh has no verb for have; possession uses a form of ‘gan’: ‘roedd llais hyfryd ganddi’ = she had a lovely voice (‘ganddi’ = with her).

target: Wyt ti eisiau bisgïen?
english: Do you want a biscuit?
tip: ‘eisiau’ (to want) normally takes no ‘yn’ linker: ‘wyt ti eisiau bisgïen?’ = do you want a biscuit, not ‘wyt ti'n eisiau’.

target: Arferai hi gerdded i'r ysgol.
english: She used to walk to school.
tip: ‘arferai’ means used to and softens the verb: ‘cerdded’ becomes ‘gerdded’, so ‘arferai hi gerdded’ = she used to walk.

target: Ga i baned o de?
english: Can I have a cup of tea?
tip: ‘ga i...?’ asks may I have...? and softens the noun: ‘paned’ becomes ‘baned’, as in ‘ga i baned o de?’

target: Alli di basio'r halen i mi?
english: Can you pass me the salt?
tip: ‘alli di...?’ means can you...? and softens the verb: ‘pasio’ becomes ‘basio’, as in ‘alli di basio'r halen?’

target: Oes beiro gyda ti alla i ddefnyddio?
english: Do you have a pen I could use?
tip: South Welsh shows possession with ‘gyda’: ‘beiro gyda ti’ = you have a pen, literally a pen with you.

target: Rhaid iddi hi gymryd y feddyginiaeth bob dydd.
english: She must take the medicine every day.
tip: ‘rhaid i’ (someone) means must, and the verb softens: ‘cymryd’ becomes ‘gymryd’, so ‘rhaid iddi hi gymryd’ = she must take.

target: Gofynnodd e i fi a oeddwn i eisiau dod.
english: He asked me if I wanted to come.
tip: here ‘a’ means whether in an indirect question: ‘gofynnodd e... a oeddwn i’ = he asked whether I was.

target: Cymraeg dw i eisiau dysgu.
english: It's Welsh that I want to learn.
tip: Front the key word for emphasis: ‘Cymraeg dw i eisiau dysgu’ = it is Welsh I want to learn, stressing ‘Cymraeg’.

target: Mae'r coffi yma'n gryfach nag ydw i'n hoffi.
english: This coffee is stronger than I like.
tip: ‘na’ before a consonant, ‘nag’ before a vowel: ‘cryfach nag ydw i’ = stronger than I am, like English a and an.

target: Roeddwn i wedi anghofio'r allweddi yn y car.
english: I had forgotten the keys in the car.
tip: ‘roedd’ plus ‘wedi’ marks a had-done past: ‘roeddwn i wedi anghofio’ = I had forgotten.

target: Roedd e wedi ysgrifennu'r llythyr ond heb ei bostio.
english: He had written the letter but hadn't posted it.
tip: ‘heb’ plus a verb means not done: ‘heb ei bostio’ = without having posted it.

target: Pe bai'r plant yn dawel, gallwn i ganolbwyntio ar y gwaith.
english: If the children were quiet, I could concentrate on the work.
tip: ‘pe bai’ sets up an unreal if: ‘pe bai'r plant yn dawel’ = if the children were quiet, implying they are not.

target: Mae hi'n canu mor brydferth ag eos.
english: She sings as beautifully as a nightingale.
tip: as...as is ‘mor’ plus adjective plus ‘â’, or ‘ag’ before a vowel: ‘mor brydferth ag eos’ = as beautiful as a nightingale.

target: Gallet ti wneud hynny.
english: You could do that.
tip: Welsh has two you forms: ‘ti’ (informal) as in ‘gallet ti’, and ‘chi’ (formal or plural).

target: Mae rhaid i ni frysio.
english: We have to hurry.
tip: After ‘rhaid i’ (someone), the verb softens: ‘brysio’ becomes ‘frysio’ in ‘rhaid i ni frysio’.

target: Rhaid i ni dorri costau.
english: We must cut costs.
tip: ‘rhaid’ itself stays the same across tenses; the ‘bod’ part changes: ‘rhaid i ni’ (must), ‘roedd rhaid i ni’ (had to).

target: Ga i weld y siwmper 'na?
english: Can I see that jumper?
tip: ‘ga i’ (may I, or can I have) softens what follows: ‘gweld’ becomes ‘ga i weld’.

target: Dylen ni adael cyn iddi dywyllu.
english: We should leave before it gets dark.
tip: ‘cyn i’ plus a subject and verb means before someone does: ‘cyn iddi dywyllu’ = before it gets dark.

target: Dylai fe ymweld â'i rieni'n amlach.
english: He should visit his parents more often.
tip: ‘dylai’ means should or ought to: ‘dylai fe ymweld’ = he should visit.

target: Ar ôl iddyn nhw fynd, eisteddais i lawr.
english: After they left, I sat down.
tip: ‘ar ôl i’ plus a subject and verb means after someone does: ‘ar ôl iddyn nhw fynd’ = after they left.

target: Mae'r llyfr yma'n fwy diddorol na'r un yna.
english: This book is more interesting than that one.
tip: ‘yma’ (this) and ‘yna’ (that) sit after the noun: ‘y llyfr yma’ = this book, ‘yr un yna’ = that one.

target: Mae'r matras newydd yn fwy cyfforddus na'r hen un.
english: The new mattress is more comfortable than the old one.
tip: For comparatives use ‘yn fwy’ (more) plus ‘na’ for than: ‘yn fwy cyfforddus na'r hen un’ = more comfortable than the old one.

target: Pe gallwn i ddewis, byddwn i'n byw ger y môr.
english: If I could choose, I would live by the sea.
tip: Unreal conditions pair ‘pe’ (if) with ‘byddwn i’ (I would): ‘pe gallwn i ddewis, byddwn i'n byw’.

target: Oes profiad gyda ti gyda chyfrifiaduron?
english: Do you have any experience with computers?
tip: The south says ‘gyda’ for have: ‘profiad gyda ti’ = you have experience; the north uses ‘gen’ or ‘gan’.

target: Fe yw'r person mwyaf cyfeillgar dw i'n nabod.
english: He's the friendliest person I know.
tip: For longer adjectives, most is ‘mwyaf’ placed before the word: ‘y person mwyaf cyfeillgar’ = the friendliest person.
